.. py:function:: aggregate_territory_measurements(territory_df: pandas.DataFrame, variable_ids: collections.abc.Sequence[str], *, agg: str = 'mean') -> pandas.DataFrame

   For each ``variable_id``, mean (or other ``agg``) ``value`` within
   ``(subject_uid, territory)``.

   Expects columns: ``subject_uid``, ``territory``, ``variable_id``, ``value``.


.. py:function:: build_analysis_df_from_repo_frames(territory_df: pandas.DataFrame, clinical_wide: pandas.DataFrame, *, imaging_variable_ids: collections.abc.Sequence[str], covariate_cols: collections.abc.Sequence[str], subject_key: str = 'subject_uid', dedupe_clinical: str = 'first', agg: str = 'mean') -> pandas.DataFrame

   One row per ``(subject_uid, territory)`` with aggregated imaging measures and
   merged covariates — same grain as ``cacs.ipynb`` after melt (long format).

   :param territory_df: Output of :func:`nvitk.stats.melt_imaging_territories`.
   :param clinical_wide: Wide clinical / joined table (e.g. ``repo.join([clinical, plaque, cognitive])``).
   :param imaging_variable_ids: ``variable_id`` values to aggregate (e.g. ``("mean_cbf", "pi")``).
   :param covariate_cols: Columns to copy from ``clinical_wide`` (must exist; typically ``tacsctot_group``,
                          ``age_at_mri``, ``sex``, …).


.. py:function:: build_analysis_df_from_territory_definitions(image_df_wide: pandas.DataFrame, clinical_wide: pandas.DataFrame, territory_definitions: collections.abc.Mapping[str, collections.abc.Mapping[str, collections.abc.Sequence[str]]], *, flow_vars: collections.abc.Sequence[str], asl_vars: collections.abc.Sequence[str], covariate_cols: collections.abc.Sequence[str], subject_key: str = 'subject_uid', dedupe_clinical: str = 'first', agg: str = 'mean', include_frame_index: bool = False) -> pandas.DataFrame

   One row per ``(subject_key, territory)`` using an **explicit** per-territory
   region list for 4D flow and ASL.

   Unlike :func:`melt_imaging_territories` + :func:`build_analysis_df_from_repo_frames`,
   the same ASL ``region_id`` (e.g. ``ctx-whole-brain``) may contribute to **more
   than one** analysis territory (e.g. ``ICA-WB`` and ``Venous-WB``) with
   different flow region groupings, because territories are not derived from a
   single inverted ``region → territory`` map.

   :param territory_definitions: ``{territory_name: {"flow": (region_ids...), "asl": (region_ids...)}}``.
                                 Either ``flow`` or ``asl`` may be omitted or empty; missing variables for
                                 that territory are filled with NaN. Region IDs must match ``region_id`` in
                                 wide column names after :func:`~nvitk.stats.parse_wide_image_column`.
   :param flow_vars: ``variable_id`` tokens to pull from wide columns (e.g. ``flow_mean``,
                     ``mean_cbf``).
   :param asl_vars: ``variable_id`` tokens to pull from wide columns (e.g. ``flow_mean``,
                    ``mean_cbf``).
   :param include_frame_index: When True, include ``flow_tseries`` (and similar) columns with ``_fN``
                               suffixes in the column index; default False matches :func:`melt_imaging_territories`.


.. py:function:: index_wide_image_columns_by_region_variable(df: pandas.DataFrame, *, id_cols: collections.abc.Sequence[str] | None = None, include_frame_index: bool = False) -> dict[tuple[str, str], list[str]]

   Map ``(region_id, variable_id)`` pairs to wide column names parseable by
   :func:`~nvitk.stats.parse_wide_image_column`.

   ``id_cols`` defaults to ``("subject_uid",)`` when present in ``df``; otherwise
   no id columns are assumed.


.. py:function:: merge_subject_covariates(long_df: pandas.DataFrame, clinical_wide: pandas.DataFrame, covariate_cols: collections.abc.Iterable[str], *, subject_key: str = 'subject_uid', dedupe: str = 'first') -> pandas.DataFrame

   Attach subject-level covariates (one row per ``subject_key`` in ``clinical_wide``).

   ``long_df`` must include ``subject_key`` and typically ``territory`` plus outcome
   columns from :func:`aggregate_territory_measurements`.

.. py:class:: MeasurementSpec

   One image measurement to load into an analysis frame.

   A spec is self-contained: it names its own pipeline kind, pipeline, feature, atlas and grouping,
   so measurements from different modalities can be combined as long as their *grouping* produces
   commensurate ``territory`` keys (e.g. qvtpy ``hemisphere`` → ``MCA``/``ACA``/``PCA`` against ASL
   ``territory`` → the same vascular-territory labels).

   :param alias: Output column name. Defaults to ``resolve_feature_id(feature)``. Must be a valid Python
                 identifier: :func:`~nvitk.stats.mixedlm.fit_or_load_mixedlm` sanitizes column names, so a
                 non-identifier alias would silently diverge between the analysis frame and the model frame.
   :type alias: str, optional


   .. py:attribute:: pipeline_kind
      :type:  str
      :value: 'qvtpy'



   .. py:attribute:: pipeline
      :type:  str
      :value: 'latest'



   .. py:attribute:: feature
      :type:  str
      :value: 'flow_mean'



   .. py:attribute:: grouping
      :type:  str
      :value: 'vessel'



   .. py:attribute:: atlas
      :type:  str | None
      :value: None



   .. py:attribute:: alias
      :type:  str | None
      :value: None



   .. py:attribute:: agg
      :type:  str
      :value: 'mean'



   .. py:attribute:: composites
      :type:  tuple[str, Ellipsis]
      :value: ()



   .. py:attribute:: regions
      :type:  tuple[str, Ellipsis]
      :value: ()



   .. py:method:: column() -> str

      Name this measurement takes in the analysis frame.



   .. py:method:: label() -> str

      One-line description for list widgets, e.g. ``"qvtpy · latest · pi · hemisphere → pi"``.



   .. py:method:: to_dict() -> dict[str, Any]

      Serialize to a JSON-safe dict.



   .. py:method:: from_dict(data: Mapping[str, Any]) -> MeasurementSpec
      :classmethod:


      Rebuild from :meth:`to_dict` output, tolerating missing keys.



.. py:function:: asl_region_id_to_hemisphere(region_id: str) -> str

   Collapse an ASL atlas region to the same vessel key the 4D-flow hemisphere grouping produces.

   ASL vascular parcels are published per side and per smoothing kernel (``left_mca_8``,
   ``right_pca_8``, ``watershed_8``). Stripping the kernel suffix and the side prefix yields
   ``MCA`` / ``ACA`` / ``PCA`` / ``ICA`` / ``Basilar`` — exactly the keys
   :func:`region_to_hemisphere_pair_key` gives for ``LMCA`` / ``RMCA`` / …, so the two modalities
   can be joined vessel by vessel rather than only at the coarse territory level.

   Watershed parcels have no 4D-flow counterpart and keep their own ``Watershed`` key; Desikan
   parcels fall back to a side-stripped parcel name.


.. py:function:: assign_group_key(region_id: str, *, grouping: str, kind: str = 'qvtpy', variable_id: str = 'flow_mean') -> str

   Map a published ``region_id`` to the analysis ``group_key``.


.. py:function:: atlas_for_request(kind: str, variable_id: str, atlas: str | None) -> str | None

   Atlas argument for ``DataRepo.image`` (ASL vascular/desikan; T1 cortical/subcortical).


.. py:function:: composites_for(kind: str, variable_id: str) -> list[tuple[str, str]]

   ``(name, label)`` composite territories available for a pipeline kind / feature.


.. py:function:: build_feature_territory_frame(repo: Any, *, pipeline_kind: str, pipeline: str, feature: str, grouping: str, atlas: str | None = None, agg: str = 'mean', column: str | None = None, composites: Sequence[str] = (), regions: Sequence[str] = ()) -> pandas.DataFrame

   One image measurement, aggregated to one row per ``(subject_uid, territory)``.

   This is the covariate-free half of :func:`build_long_analysis_frame`: it loads the long-form
   rows for a single ``variable_id``, assigns the ``territory`` group key implied by *grouping*, and
   aggregates within each ``(subject_uid, territory)`` cell. Keeping it separate is what lets
   several measurements from *different* pipelines be joined on a shared key before any covariate
   merge happens — attaching covariates per measurement would compound their inner merge.

   :param pipeline_kind: Selects the imaging modality via :data:`KIND_MODALITY`.
   :type pipeline_kind: {"qvtpy", "asl", "t1", "flair", "tof"}
   :param pipeline: Pipeline id, or one of ``latest``/``default``/``current``/``last`` for the catalog default.
   :type pipeline: str
   :param feature: Feature name or alias; resolved through :func:`resolve_feature_id`.
   :type feature: str
   :param grouping: How ``region_id`` collapses into ``territory`` (see :func:`assign_group_key`).
   :type grouping: GroupingMode
   :param agg: Aggregation applied within each ``(subject_uid, territory)`` cell.
   :type agg: str
   :param column: Output column name. Defaults to the resolved ``variable_id``.
   :type column: str, optional
   :param composites: Names from :data:`COMPOSITE_DEFINITIONS` to append as extra territory labels, e.g.
                      ``("TCBF",)``. They are computed from the raw ``region_id`` rows, so they are unaffected by
                      *grouping*, and appear as additional levels of ``territory``.
   :type composites: sequence of str
   :param regions: Keep only these published ``region_id``s. Empty means all. Matching is case-insensitive and
                   ignores ``-``/``_`` differences, because the same structure is spelled several ways across
                   importers.

                   The filter runs *after* composites are built, so naming ``TCBF`` here keeps the composite
                   while dropping the vessels it was summed from — which is the point of asking for it. It is
                   what makes a whole-head scalar usable: ``t1_volume_mm3`` publishes 61 regions, of which
                   ``etiv`` is one, and a model wanting head size wants that row and no other.
   :type regions: sequence of str

   :returns: Columns ``subject_uid``, ``territory``, and the measurement column.
             ``frame.attrs["region_ids"]`` lists the source region ids, which lets callers work out
             whether a different grouping would produce keys compatible with another measurement.
   :rtype: pandas.DataFrame


.. py:function:: build_long_analysis_frame(repo: Any, *, pipeline_kind: str, pipeline: str, feature: str, grouping: str, atlas: str | None = None, clinical_vars: list[str] | None = None, cognitive_vars: list[str] | None = None) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Load long-form image rows, assign group keys, aggregate, attach covariates.

   Single-measurement convenience wrapper over :func:`build_multi_feature_analysis_frame`.


.. py:function:: build_multi_feature_analysis_frame(repo: Any, *, measurements: Sequence[MeasurementSpec | Mapping[str, Any]], clinical_vars: list[str] | None = None, cognitive_vars: list[str] | None = None, join: str = 'inner', grain: str = 'territory', attach_qc: bool = True) -> tuple[pandas.DataFrame, dict[str, Any]]

   Analysis frame combining one or more image measurements plus subject covariates.

   Each measurement is loaded independently by :func:`build_feature_territory_frame` and the
   results are joined on ``(subject_uid, territory)``. With ``join="inner"`` (the default) only
   subject/territory cells present in *every* measurement survive, which is the right grain for a
   model like ``att_mean ~ pi + …``: every row then has all its predictors observed.

   Covariates are merged **once**, after the measurement join. The covariate merge is an inner
   merge on ``subject_uid``, so attaching it per measurement would apply it repeatedly.

   :param join: How successive measurement frames are combined.
   :type join: {"inner", "outer", "left"}
   :param grain: What a row is. ``"territory"`` keeps the long shape and joins on the shared
                 ``(subject, territory)`` cell — right when the measurements share a parcellation, and the
                 only way to fit a model with a territory term. ``"subject"`` gives one row per subject and
                 spreads each measurement's territories into ``value@territory`` columns, which is the only
                 way to relate measurements whose parcellations name different kinds of region: an ASL
                 whole-brain CBF against a 4D-flow vessel, or a FreeSurfer parcel against either.
   :type grain: {"territory", "subject"}
   :param attach_qc: Merge the published per-vessel autoQC metrics (``qc_flow_plausible``, ``qc_score``, …) onto
                     the frame. They are what the QC filter presets read, so turning this off greys those out —
                     but it also keeps five columns nobody asked for out of a frame built for something else,
                     and skips their lookup on a dataset where the stage never ran.
   :type attach_qc: bool

   :returns: *meta* carries ``measurements`` (per-spec row/subject/territory counts), ``key_overlap``
             (fraction of measurement 0's keys retained after each join), ``n_rows``, ``covariates``, and
             ``warnings`` — a list of human-readable problems worth surfacing in a UI, most importantly a
             disjoint ``territory`` vocabulary between two pipelines.
   :rtype: (frame, meta)

   :raises ValueError: If *measurements* is empty or two specs would write the same output column.


.. py:function:: collapse_visits_to_subject(frame: pandas.DataFrame, *, policy: str = 'latest', subject_key: str = 'subject_uid', visit_key: str = 'visit_id') -> tuple[pandas.DataFrame, dict[str, list[str]]]

   Collapse a per-visit measurement frame to one row per subject, combining across visits.

   ``clinical_measurements`` pivots on ``(subject_uid, visit_id)``, so a cohort whose variables were
   collected at different visits gets one row per visit with the *other* visits' variables blank.
   Anything downstream that assumes one row per subject then keeps a single visit and silently
   discards the rest — which is how requesting carotid plaque (visit 3) alongside the rest of the
   clinical panel (visit 4) can null out the panel.

   Each column is filled from the first non-missing value in visit order, so variables measured at
   different visits combine instead of competing.

   :param policy: Which visit wins for a variable recorded at more than one. ``latest`` takes the most recent.
   :type policy: {"latest", "earliest"}

   :returns: *provenance* maps each column to the visits that contributed a value, so a caller can tell
             the user which variables came from where.
   :rtype: (collapsed, provenance)


.. py:function:: feature_family(kind: str, variable_id: str) -> str

   Return ``vessel`` / ``tree`` / ``region`` for grouping UI defaults.


.. py:function:: features_for_kind(kind: str) -> list[str]

   List the available feature ``variable_id``s for a pipeline kind (qvtpy/asl/t1/flair/tof).


.. py:function:: finalize_analysis_frame(wide: pandas.DataFrame, repo: Any, *, primary_variable_id: str | None = None) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Add the conveniences every Statmodels frame is expected to carry.

   In order: ``group_key`` (a copy of ``territory``, used as the default MixedLM grouping), the
   friendly outcome aliases the default formulas reference (``flow`` for ``flow_mean``, and the
   inverse of :data:`FEATURE_ALIASES`), ``patient_id``, the ``hematocrit`` → ``Hematocrit`` rename,
   numeric coercion of catalog-numeric covariates, and the mean-centered ``age_c``.

   :param primary_variable_id: Measurement to alias. With several measurements loaded, only the first one gets aliases —
                               the aliases exist for the legacy single-feature default formulas.
   :type primary_variable_id: str, optional


.. py:function:: grouping_choices_for(kind: str, variable_id: str) -> list[tuple[str, str]]

   Ordered ``(label, key)`` grouping options for the current modality/feature.


.. py:function:: region_to_hemisphere_pair_key(region_id: str) -> str

   Collapse L/R counterparts to one key (ICA, MCA, …); midline stays itself.

   The result is canonicalized through :data:`_HEMISPHERE_CANONICAL`, so spellings that differ only
   in separator or case land on the same key. That is what lets a 4D-flow measurement grouped by
   hemisphere join an ASL one on ``(subject_uid, territory)``.


.. py:function:: t1_region_to_hemisphere_pair_key(region_id: str) -> str

   Drop the hemisphere prefix from a FreeSurfer region so L/R counterparts share a key.

   ``left_precuneus`` and ``right_precuneus`` both become ``precuneus``; midline structures
   (``brain_stem``, ``csf``) and the whole-head scalars (``etiv``) are returned unchanged.

   Kept separate from :func:`region_to_hemisphere_pair_key` because that one is built for vessels:
   it canonicalizes through the vessel table and upper-cases short names, which would turn
   ``left_bankssts`` into ``BANKSSTS`` and leave the hemisphere grouping spelled unlike every other
   T1 grouping. Parcel names have no canonical short form, so stripping the side is all there is
   to do.

   .. rubric:: Examples

   >>> t1_region_to_hemisphere_pair_key("left_precuneus")
   'precuneus'
   >>> t1_region_to_hemisphere_pair_key("brain_stem")
   'brain_stem'


.. py:function:: resolve_covariate_frame(repo: Any, *, clinical_vars: list[str] | None = None, cognitive_vars: list[str] | None = None, visit_policy: str = 'latest') -> tuple[pandas.DataFrame, list[str]]

   Subject-level covariate frame assembled from the clinical / subjects / image / cognitive tables.

   Each source is collapsed to one row per subject (see :func:`collapse_visits_to_subject`) *before*
   the sources are merged, so variables recorded at different visits combine rather than
   multiplying rows or shadowing one another.

   :returns: *covariates* is one row per ``subject_uid`` (outer-merged across sources, duplicated columns
             dropped from the right frame); *present* lists the requested names that actually resolved.
             ``covariates.attrs["visit_provenance"]`` maps each column to the visits it came from.
             A source that raises is skipped silently — a missing cognitive table must not block a model
             that only needs clinical covariates.
   :rtype: (covariates, present)


.. py:function:: resolve_feature_id(feature: str) -> str

   Resolve a friendly feature alias (e.g. ``"flow"``) to its canonical ``variable_id`` (e.g. ``"flow_mean"``).


.. py:function:: subject_attribute_columns(repo: Any) -> list[str]

   ``variable_id``s of the subject-level covariates returned by :func:`subject_attribute_entries`.


.. py:function:: subject_attribute_entries(repo: Any) -> list[dict[str, Any]]

   Subject-level covariates (``sex``, …) available on the ``subjects`` table, in the same
   ``{"variable_id", "label", "domain"}`` shape as :meth:`Catalog.variable_entries`.

   Bookkeeping / identifier / timestamp columns are excluded, as are names already available as
   clinical measurements (catalog entry **or** rows in ``clinical_measurements``) — the measurement
   table always wins over the entity column.


.. py:function:: subject_image_annotation_columns(repo: Any) -> list[str]

   ``variable_id``s of the subject-level image annotations offered as covariates.


.. py:function:: subject_image_annotation_entries(repo: Any) -> list[dict[str, Any]]

   Image variables holding **one value per subject** rather than one per vessel.

   These are the manual QC annotations — ``cow_config`` / ``venous_config``, see
   :mod:`nvitk.db.qvtpy_anatomy` — which describe the subject's anatomy as a whole and so carry no
   ``region_id``. They cannot be measurements in an analysis frame (there is no region to join on),
   but they are exactly what a model wants as a subject-level factor, so they are offered
   alongside the clinical covariates.

   Recognized by ``scope == "subject"`` on the catalog entry, plus the known annotation ids —
   a dataset whose catalog was written by an older run may carry the rows without the flag.


.. py:function:: clinical_measurement_variable_ids(repo: Any) -> set[str]

   ``variable_id``s that currently have at least one row in ``clinical_measurements``.

   Used to prefer the measurements table over the sparse ``subjects`` entity columns when both
   expose the same name (e.g. ``sex`` after ``import_sex.py``). Catalog registration alone is not
   enough: a Statmodels window opened before the import keeps a stale catalog and would otherwise
   keep routing ``sex`` through ``subjects``.


.. py:data:: DEFAULT_IQR_K
   :value: 1.5


.. py:data:: FILTER_OPS
   :value: ('>', '>=', '<', '<=', '==', '!=', 'contains', 'equals')


.. py:data:: IDENTIFIER_RE

.. py:data:: TRANSFORM_LABELS
   :type:  dict[str, str]

.. py:data:: TRANSFORMS
   :type:  dict[str, Callable[[pandas.Series], pandas.Series]]

.. py:class:: DerivedColumn

   A column computed from the analysis frame.

   :param name: Output column name. Must be a valid identifier — see :data:`IDENTIFIER_RE`.
   :type name: str
   :param kind: ``transform`` applies :data:`TRANSFORMS`\ ``[transform]`` to *source*;
                ``expression`` evaluates *expression* via :func:`evaluate_expression`;
                ``bins`` cuts *source* into an ordered categorical at *cut_points*, the
                ``tacsctot`` → ``tacsctot_group`` pattern;
                ``merge`` pools levels of a categorical *source* into fewer groups via *mapping*, the
                ``apoe`` → ``E4_carrier`` / ``E2_carrier`` / ``E3E3`` pattern.
   :type kind: {"transform", "expression", "bins", "merge"}
   :param mapping: For ``kind="merge"``: which source level goes into which new group. Stored as pairs rather
                   than a dict so the definition round-trips through JSON with a stable order.
   :type mapping: tuple of (level, group)
   :param unmapped: What happens to a level not named in *mapping*: ``"keep"`` leaves it under its own name,
                    ``"drop"`` makes it missing, or any other string is used as a catch-all group label.
   :type unmapped: str
   :param cut_points: Interior cut points for ``kind="bins"``. The bins are bracketed by ±∞, so ``(0, 25, 100)``
                      gives four groups: ``≤ 0``, ``(0, 25]``, ``(25, 100]``, ``> 100``.
   :type cut_points: tuple of float
   :param labels: Explicit bin labels. When empty, ``label_prefix`` + index is used.
   :type labels: tuple of str


   .. py:attribute:: name
      :type:  str


   .. py:attribute:: kind
      :type:  str
      :value: 'transform'



   .. py:attribute:: source
      :type:  str
      :value: ''



   .. py:attribute:: transform
      :type:  str
      :value: ''



   .. py:attribute:: expression
      :type:  str
      :value: ''



   .. py:attribute:: cut_points
      :type:  tuple[float, Ellipsis]
      :value: ()



   .. py:attribute:: labels
      :type:  tuple[str, Ellipsis]
      :value: ()



   .. py:attribute:: label_prefix
      :type:  str
      :value: 'g'



   .. py:attribute:: right
      :type:  bool
      :value: True



   .. py:attribute:: mapping
      :type:  tuple[tuple[str, str], Ellipsis]
      :value: ()



   .. py:attribute:: unmapped
      :type:  str
      :value: 'keep'



   .. py:method:: n_bins() -> int

      Number of bins this definition produces (one more than the interior cut points).



   .. py:method:: bin_labels() -> tuple[str, Ellipsis]

      Labels for each bin — the explicit ones when given, else ``prefix0``, ``prefix1``, …



   .. py:method:: merge_groups() -> dict[str, list[str]]

      ``{new group: [source levels]}``, in the order the groups were first named.



   .. py:method:: label() -> str

      Human-readable definition, e.g. ``"cp_group = bins(lcp: 0, 25, 100)"``.



   .. py:method:: validate() -> str

      Return an error message describing why this column is unusable, or ``""`` if it is fine.



   .. py:method:: to_dict() -> dict[str, Any]

      Serialize to a JSON-safe dict.



   .. py:method:: from_dict(data: Mapping[str, Any]) -> DerivedColumn
      :classmethod:


      Rebuild from :meth:`to_dict` output, tolerating missing keys.



.. py:class:: FilterRule

   One declarative row filter over a single column.

   :param column: Column the rule is anchored to.
   :type column: str
   :param kind: ``values``  keep/exclude an explicit set of levels (the vessel-exclusion case);
                ``compare`` apply *op* / *value* through :func:`apply_row_filter`;
                ``range``   keep rows inside ``[low, high]``;
                ``iqr``     drop Tukey-fence outliers, optionally per level of *by*.
   :type kind: {"values", "compare", "range", "iqr"}
   :param enabled: Disabled rules are kept (so the UI can toggle them) but contribute no filtering.
   :type enabled: bool


   .. py:attribute:: column
      :type:  str


   .. py:attribute:: kind
      :type:  str


   .. py:attribute:: op
      :type:  str
      :value: '=='



   .. py:attribute:: value
      :type:  str
      :value: ''



   .. py:attribute:: values
      :type:  tuple[str, Ellipsis]
      :value: ()



   .. py:attribute:: exclude
      :type:  bool
      :value: False



   .. py:attribute:: low
      :type:  float | None
      :value: None



   .. py:attribute:: high
      :type:  float | None
      :value: None



   .. py:attribute:: keep_na
      :type:  bool
      :value: False



   .. py:attribute:: k
      :type:  float
      :value: 1.5



   .. py:attribute:: by
      :type:  str | None
      :value: None



   .. py:attribute:: enabled
      :type:  bool
      :value: True



   .. py:method:: label() -> str

      Short human-readable description, used as the chip text in the GUI.



   .. py:method:: to_dict() -> dict[str, Any]

      Serialize to a JSON-safe dict (tuples become lists).



   .. py:method:: from_dict(data: Mapping[str, Any]) -> FilterRule
      :classmethod:


      Rebuild a rule from :meth:`to_dict` output, tolerating missing keys.



.. py:function:: apply_derived_columns(df: pandas.DataFrame, columns: Sequence[DerivedColumn]) -> tuple[pandas.DataFrame, list[str]]

   Append each derived column to a copy of *df*, in list order.

   Later entries may reference earlier ones, so ``log_pi`` then ``z_log_pi`` works. A column that
   fails (bad name, missing source, broken expression) is skipped and its error collected; the rest
   still land, so one typo does not cost the whole set.

   :rtype: (frame, errors)


.. py:function:: apply_filter_rules(df: pandas.DataFrame, rules: Sequence[FilterRule]) -> tuple[pandas.DataFrame, list[dict[str, Any]]]

   Apply *rules* to *df* in order, reporting the effect of each.

   :param df: Frame to filter. Never mutated.
   :type df: pandas.DataFrame
   :param rules: Applied left to right; each sees the output of the previous one.
   :type rules: sequence of FilterRule

   :returns: *report* has one entry per rule: ``{"rule", "n_before", "n_after", "removed", "skipped",
             "reason"}``. A rule referencing a column that is not in the frame is skipped with
             ``reason="column not in frame"`` and removes nothing — a saved filter set must not silently
             empty a frame whose columns changed.
   :rtype: (filtered, report)


.. py:function:: apply_iqr_filter(df: pandas.DataFrame, column: str, *, k: float = DEFAULT_IQR_K, by: str | None = None) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Drop rows whose *column* value falls outside the Tukey fences ``[Q1 - k·IQR, Q3 + k·IQR]``.

   With *by* set, the fences are computed within each level of that column. That is the meaningful
   scope for image measurements, whose magnitude depends on the region: a global fence is driven by
   the spread *between* regions rather than within them, so it misses real outliers inside each
   region and — when one region sits far from the rest — can discard that region wholesale. Rows
   with a missing value are kept; dropping them is the fit's job, not the filter's.


.. py:function:: apply_row_filter(df: pandas.DataFrame, column: str, op: str, value: str) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Filter *df* to rows where *column* satisfies *op* against *value* (numeric comparisons,
   substring/exact string match, or equality/inequality); returns *df* unchanged if *column* is
   missing or blank.


.. py:function:: bin_counts(series: pandas.Series, spec: DerivedColumn) -> pandas.Series

   Rows falling in each bin of *spec*, in bin order — the preview that makes cut points checkable.


.. py:function:: bin_interval_labels(cut_points: Sequence[float], *, right: bool = True) -> list[str]

   Human-readable interval for each bin, e.g. ``["≤ 0", "(0, 25]", "(25, 100]", "> 100"]``.

   The bins are always bracketed by ±∞, so every finite value lands in exactly one of them and
   nothing is silently dropped for being off the end of the scale.


.. py:function:: cut_into_bins(series: pandas.Series, cut_points: Sequence[float], labels: Sequence[str], *, right: bool = True) -> pandas.Series

   Bin a continuous *series* into an **ordered** categorical.

   The bins are ``(-inf, c0]``, ``(c0, c1]``, …, ``(cn, +inf)`` when *right* is true, so a value
   equal to a cut point falls in the lower bin — which is what makes "exactly 0" its own group when
   ``0`` is the first cut point.

   Ordered rather than plain categorical: patsy then treats the first label as the reference level
   and plots keep the bins in their natural sequence rather than alphabetically.


.. py:function:: default_bin_labels(n_bins: int, prefix: str) -> tuple[str, Ellipsis]

   ``("cp0", "cp1", …)`` for *n_bins* bins — the ``tacsctot_group`` convention.


.. py:function:: default_bin_name(source: str) -> str

   Conventional name for a binned column, mirroring ``tacsctot`` → ``tacsctot_group``.


.. py:function:: default_derived_name(source: str, transform: str) -> str

   Conventional name for a canned transform, e.g. ``("pi", "log") -> "log_pi"``.


.. py:function:: evaluate_expression(df: pandas.DataFrame, expression: str) -> pandas.Series

   Evaluate *expression* against *df*'s columns and return the resulting series.

   The expression is compiled and evaluated with ``__builtins__`` stripped and a namespace holding
   only the frame's columns plus :data:`_SAFE_NAMESPACE`. That blocks the obvious mistakes
   (``__import__``, ``open``) but is **not** a sandbox — an expression is code the user typed, and
   should be treated with the same trust as the rest of the session. Expressions restored from a
   config file that the user did not author must be confirmed before evaluation.

   :raises ValueError: If the expression is blank, fails to compile/evaluate, or does not produce a value that can
       be aligned to *df*'s index.


.. py:function:: filtered_columns(rules: Sequence[FilterRule]) -> set[str]

   Columns touched by at least one enabled rule (used to badge table headers).


.. py:function:: parse_cut_points(text: str) -> tuple[float, Ellipsis]

   Parse a comma/space separated list of interior cut points, e.g. ``"0, 25, 100"``.

   :raises ValueError: If a token is not a number, or the points are not strictly increasing — overlapping or
       repeated edges would make the bin a value falls into ambiguous.


.. py:function:: suggest_cut_points(series: pandas.Series, *, method: str, n_bins: int = 4) -> tuple[float, Ellipsis]

   Propose interior cut points for *series*.

   The result is meant to be written into the definition as explicit numbers, not recomputed on
   every load: cut points derived live from the data would shift whenever a filter changed, so the
   same named group would mean different things between two fits.

   :param method:
   :type method: {"quantile", "equal_width"}
   :param n_bins: Number of bins wanted; ``n_bins - 1`` interior cut points are returned.
   :type n_bins: int

   :type:  dict[str, str]

   :value: ('mixedlm_bootstrap', 'pingouin_by_level', 'statsmodels_parametric')


.. py:data:: POOLED_OLS_NOTE
   :value: 'This engine fits pooled OLS models: repeated (subject × territory) rows are treated as...


.. py:class:: MediationSpec

   One mediation analysis: which columns play which role, and how to estimate it.

   :param x: Exposure, mediator, outcome column names. These must be bare frame columns — a transformed
             term belongs in a derived column, not here, because the engines look coefficients up by name.
   :type x: str
   :param m: Exposure, mediator, outcome column names. These must be bare frame columns — a transformed
             term belongs in a derived column, not here, because the engines look coefficients up by name.
   :type m: str
   :param y: Exposure, mediator, outcome column names. These must be bare frame columns — a transformed
             term belongs in a derived column, not here, because the engines look coefficients up by name.
   :type y: str
   :param covariates: Adjusted for in both the mediator and the outcome model.
   :type covariates: tuple of str
   :param group_col: Nesting level: the MixedLM ``groups`` for ``mixedlm_bootstrap``, the split column for
                     ``pingouin_by_level``. Ignored by ``statsmodels_parametric``.
   :type group_col: str
   :param subject_col: Cluster resampled by ``mixedlm_bootstrap`` and used as its variance component.
   :type subject_col: str
   :param n_boot: Bootstrap draws (``n_rep`` for ``statsmodels_parametric``).
   :type n_boot: int


   .. py:attribute:: x
      :type:  str


   .. py:attribute:: m
      :type:  str


   .. py:attribute:: y
      :type:  str


   .. py:attribute:: covariates
      :type:  tuple[str, Ellipsis]
      :value: ()



   .. py:attribute:: group_col
      :type:  str
      :value: 'territory'



   .. py:attribute:: subject_col
      :type:  str
      :value: 'subject_uid'



   .. py:attribute:: engine
      :type:  str
      :value: 'mixedlm_bootstrap'



   .. py:attribute:: n_boot
      :type:  int
      :value: 500



   .. py:attribute:: seed
      :type:  int
      :value: 42



   .. py:attribute:: ci
      :type:  float
      :value: 0.95



   .. py:method:: formulas() -> tuple[str, str]

      ``(mediator_formula, outcome_formula)`` — ``m ~ x + covars`` and ``y ~ m + x + covars``.



   .. py:method:: required_columns() -> list[str]

      Every column the analysis touches, de-duplicated in a stable order.



   .. py:method:: validate(df: pandas.DataFrame | None = None) -> str

      Return why this spec cannot be run, or ``""`` if it is usable.



   .. py:method:: to_dict() -> dict[str, Any]

      Serialize to a JSON-safe dict.



   .. py:method:: from_dict(data: Mapping[str, Any]) -> MediationSpec
      :classmethod:


      Rebuild from :meth:`to_dict` output, tolerating missing keys.



.. py:function:: bootstrap_mediation_by_subject(df, formula_m, formula_y, model_cols, n_boot=500, seed=42)

   Mediation bootstrap (a*b) resampling at the subject level.

   Deprecated
   ----------
   Kept for the ``nvitk.stats.mediation`` catalog entry and existing notebooks. It hardcodes
   ``x="pi"``, ``m="pp"`` and ``groups="territory"``; prefer
   :func:`bootstrap_mediation_mixedlm_by_subject`, which takes them as arguments.

   :returns:     - indirect_dist (np.array)
                 - ci_low, ci_high
                 - mean
                 - p_value (two-sided bootstrap)
   :rtype: dict with


.. py:function:: bootstrap_mediation_mixedlm_by_subject(df: pandas.DataFrame, *, formula_m: str, formula_y: str, x: str, m: str, y: str, group_col: str = 'territory', subject_col: str = 'subject_uid', required_columns: Sequence[str] | None = None, n_boot: int = 500, seed: int = 42, re_formula: str = '1', vc_formula: dict[str, str] | None = None, fit_kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None, ci: float = 0.95, return_dist: bool = True, progress: Callable[[int, int], None] | None = None, should_cancel: Callable[[], bool] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

   Cluster-bootstrap mediation for MixedLM models, resampling whole subjects.

   Strategy
   --------
   1. Fit both models once on the observed data for the point estimates
      (``a = coef of x in M``, ``b = coef of m in Y``, ``c' = coef of x in Y``).
   2. For each draw, resample *subjects* with replacement and keep **all** of each subject's rows
      (its territories), relabeling the ids so a repeated subject forms a distinct variance-component
      group. Refit both models and record ``a·b``, ``c'`` and their sum.
   3. Summarize each path by its percentile interval and a two-sided bootstrap p-value.

   Resampling whole subjects — rather than rows — is what keeps the within-subject correlation in
   the resampled data; row-wise resampling would understate the uncertainty.

   :param formula_m: Mediator and outcome model formulas, e.g. ``"pi ~ pp + age_c + sex"`` and
                     ``"att_mean ~ pi + pp + age_c + sex"``. See :meth:`MediationSpec.formulas`.
   :type formula_m: str
   :param formula_y: Mediator and outcome model formulas, e.g. ``"pi ~ pp + age_c + sex"`` and
                     ``"att_mean ~ pi + pp + age_c + sex"``. See :meth:`MediationSpec.formulas`.
   :type formula_y: str
   :param vc_formula: Variance components. Defaults to ``{"subject": f"0 + C({subject_col})"}``.
   :type vc_formula: dict, optional
   :param progress: Called as ``progress(done, total)`` after every draw.
   :type progress: callable, optional
   :param should_cancel: Polled every draw; when it returns ``True`` the run stops early and the result carries
                         ``cancelled=True`` with whatever draws completed.
   :type should_cancel: callable, optional

   :returns: ``point_estimate`` (a, b, c_prime, indirect, direct, total), ``bootstrap`` (per-path
             ``mean``/``ci_low``/``ci_high``/``p_value``/``n``), ``dist`` (draw arrays, when
             *return_dist*), ``n_boot``, ``n_failed_draws``, ``cancelled``.
   :rtype: dict

   :raises ValueError: If the observed-data fits do not expose *x* / *m* as named parameters — which happens when a
       term is wrapped (``C(x)``) or transformed in the formula. The message lists what is available.


.. py:function:: mediation_boot_to_stats_df(boot_res: dict[str, Any], *, include_total: bool = True) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Convert :func:`bootstrap_mediation_mixedlm_by_subject` output into a tidy path table.


.. py:function:: mediation_result_frame(result: Any, *, engine: str, level: str | None = None) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Normalize any engine's output to the tidy path table.

   Accepts the bootstrap result *dict* from :func:`bootstrap_mediation_mixedlm_by_subject` or an
   already-tidy frame from the pingouin / statsmodels engines.


.. py:function:: pingouin_mediation(df: pandas.DataFrame, *, x: str, m: str, y: str, covar: Sequence[str] = (), n_boot: int = 5000, seed: int = 42, alpha: float = 0.05) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Single ``pingouin.mediation_analysis`` run, normalized to the tidy path table.


.. py:function:: pingouin_mediation_by_level(df: pandas.DataFrame, *, x: str, m: str, y: str, covar: Sequence[str] = (), level_col: str = 'territory', n_boot: int = 5000, seed: int = 42, alpha: float = 0.05, min_rows: int | None = None, dropna: bool = True, progress: Callable[[int, int], None] | None = None, should_cancel: Callable[[], bool] | None = None) -> tuple[dict[str, pandas.DataFrame], pandas.DataFrame]

   Run :func:`pingouin_mediation` separately within each level of *level_col*.

   Levels with too few complete rows to fit the models are skipped: with *min_rows* unset the
   threshold is ``max(20, 5 + 3·len(covar))``, which scales with the number of parameters.

   :returns: *by_level* maps each level to its tidy path table; *summary* has one row per level with the
             indirect / direct / total effects and their intervals, sorted by indirect effect.
   :rtype: (by_level, summary)


.. py:function:: plot_indirect_bootstrap(dist: Sequence[float], *, ci_low: float | None = None, ci_high: float | None = None, ax: Any | None = None, bins: int = 50) -> Any

   Histogram + KDE of the bootstrap distribution of the indirect effect, with CI markers.


.. py:function:: plot_indirect_by_level(summary_df: pandas.DataFrame, *, ax: Any | None = None, level_col: str = 'level') -> Any

   Forest plot of the indirect effect within each grouping level.


.. py:function:: plot_mediation_forest(stats_df: pandas.DataFrame, *, ax: Any | None = None, title: str = 'Mediation path estimates', order: Sequence[str] = _PATH_ORDER) -> Any

   Forest plot of path coefficients with their confidence intervals.


.. py:function:: plot_partial_paths_mediation(df: pandas.DataFrame, *, x: str, m: str, y: str, covars: Sequence[str] = (), figsize: tuple[float, float] = (12, 5)) -> Any

   Partial-regression plots of the ``a`` and ``b`` paths.

   Left: ``m`` against ``x``, both residualized on the covariates. Right: ``y`` against ``m``, both
   residualized on ``x`` + covariates — the adjusted relationship the ``b`` coefficient describes.
   These are OLS partial plots, offered as a visual check rather than as the mixed-model estimate.


.. py:function:: render_mediation_info(bundle: Mapping[str, Any]) -> str

   Fixed-width text report of a :func:`run_mediation` bundle, for the report panel's Raw tab.


.. py:function:: run_mediation(df: pandas.DataFrame, spec: MediationSpec, *, progress: Callable[[int, int], None] | None = None, should_cancel: Callable[[], bool] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

   Run the engine named by *spec* and return a uniform result bundle.

   :returns: ``spec``, ``engine``, ``paths`` (the tidy table), ``by_level`` and ``summary`` (per-level
             engine only), ``raw`` (the engine's native output), and ``note`` (a caveat to surface, or
             ``""``).
   :rtype: dict


.. py:function:: statsmodels_mediation(df: pandas.DataFrame, *, x: str, m: str, y: str, covariates: Sequence[str] = (), method: str = 'parametric', n_rep: int = 1000, seed: int = 42) -> pandas.DataFrame

   ``statsmodels.stats.mediation.Mediation`` with OLS mediator and outcome models.

   The models are fitted on the pooled frame, so repeated (subject × territory) rows count as
   independent observations — see :data:`POOLED_OLS_NOTE`, which is attached to the returned frame
   as ``frame.attrs["note"]``.

   :param method: Passed to ``Mediation.fit``.
   :type method: {"parametric", "bootstrap"}

.. py:function:: covariance_term(structure: str, visit: str, subject: str, *, group: str = '') -> str

   Render a covariance term on its own, e.g. ``us(territory | subject_uid)``.

   Split out from :func:`mmrm_formula` so a UI can offer the term for insertion into a formula the
   user is writing, rather than only assembling a whole formula.

   :param group: Optional grouping column for a *separate* covariance matrix per group, written
                 ``us(visit | group / subject)``.
   :type group: str


.. py:function:: fit_mmrm(*, data: pandas.DataFrame, formula: str, visit: str = '', subject: str = '', structure: str = 'us', group: str = '', method: str = 'Satterthwaite', reml: bool = True, strict: bool = True) -> tuple[Any, pandas.DataFrame, dict[str, Any]]

   Fit a mixed model for repeated measures.

   :param formula: Either the full R formula with the covariance term written inline —
                   ``"pi ~ age_c + us(territory | mri_id)"`` — or the fixed part alone, in which case the term
                   is assembled from *visit*, *subject*, *structure* and *group*. An inline term always wins:
                   if you wrote one, that is the model, and the separate arguments are ignored.
   :type formula: str
   :param method: Denominator degrees of freedom; see :data:`DF_METHODS`.
   :type method: str
   :param reml: Restricted maximum likelihood. Leave on unless comparing fixed-effects specifications by
                likelihood.
   :type reml: bool
   :param strict: Refuse to fit when :func:`validate_mmrm_data` finds a hard problem. Set ``False`` to
                  downgrade those to warnings.
   :type strict: bool

   :returns: *fit* is the R ``mmrm`` object; *metadata* matches the other engines.
   :rtype: (fit, model_df, metadata)


.. py:function:: mmrm_backend_status(*, check_r_packages: bool = True) -> MmrmBackendStatus

   Probe rpy2 → R → ``mmrm``. Never raises, and never imports R as an import side effect.

   Deliberately independent of the lme4 probe: MMRM needs neither pymer4 nor the easystats suite,
   so it can be available when the lme4 engine is not, and reporting them together would send you
   chasing packages you do not need.


.. py:function:: mmrm_coef_frame(fit: Any) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Fixed-effects table, normalized to this package's column names.


.. py:function:: mmrm_correlation_matrix(fit: Any) -> pandas.DataFrame

   The covariance matrix rescaled to correlations.

   This is the thing an unstructured MMRM is *for*: it says how alike two territories actually are,
   which a random intercept assumes rather than estimates.


.. py:function:: mmrm_covariance_matrix(fit: Any) -> pandas.DataFrame

   The estimated covariance matrix of the repeated measures, indexed by level.


.. py:function:: mmrm_emmeans(fit: Any, specs: str) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Least-squares means from ``emmeans``, as a tidy frame.

   :param specs: An emmeans specification formula, e.g. ``"~ territory"`` or
                 ``"~ tacsctot_group | territory"``.
   :type specs: str

   :returns: The grid columns plus ``emmean``, ``SE``, ``df``, ``lower.CL``, ``upper.CL``.
   :rtype: pandas.DataFrame


.. py:function:: mmrm_formula(fixed: str, *, visit: str, subject: str, structure: str = 'us', group: str = '') -> str

   Append an ``mmrm`` covariance term to a fixed-effects formula.

   >>> mmrm_formula("pi ~ age_c + sex", visit="territory", subject="subject_uid")
   'pi ~ age_c + sex + us(territory | subject_uid)'

   :param group: Optional grouping column for a *separate* covariance matrix per group, written
                 ``us(visit | group / subject)`` — e.g. one covariance per treatment arm.
   :type group: str


.. py:function:: mmrm_info_dict(fit: Any, *, outcome_name: str = 'Outcome', meta: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

   Report structure matching the other engines, so the shared panel renders it unchanged.


.. py:function:: parse_mmrm_covariance(formula: str) -> tuple[str, CovarianceTerm | None]

   Split an ``mmrm`` formula into its fixed part and its covariance term.

   Lets the term be written inline — ``… + us(territory | mri_id)`` — the way it is in R, instead
   of being assembled from separate controls. Returns the fixed formula with the term removed, plus
   the parsed term (``None`` when the formula has none).

   >>> parse_mmrm_covariance("pi ~ age_c + us(territory | mri_id)")[1].subject
   'mri_id'


.. py:function:: mmrm_random_effects_frame(fit: Any) -> pandas.DataFrame

   The covariance structure rendered as component/kind/var/sd rows.

   Lets an MMRM reuse the shared report panel's "Random effects" tab: the diagonal becomes one
   variance per level, and the off-diagonal correlations follow.


.. py:function:: plot_mmrm_correlation(fit: Any, *, levels: Sequence[str] | None = None, title: str = 'Estimated correlation between levels') -> Any

   Heatmap of the estimated correlation matrix.

   Worth looking at whenever the structure is unstructured: it shows directly whether the compound
   symmetry a random-intercept model would have assumed is anywhere near the truth.

   :param levels: Show only these levels, in this order. The correlations are still *estimated* over every
                  level — this only restricts the display.
   :type levels: sequence of str, optional


.. py:function:: plot_mmrm_emmeans(emmeans_frame: pandas.DataFrame, *, x: str, hue: str | None = None, errorbar: bool = True, palette: str = 'tab10', display: str = 'overview', title: str = 'MMRM least-squares means', y_label: str = 'Estimated marginal mean') -> Any

   Least-squares means with their confidence intervals, drawn like the other categorical plots.

   Whiskers rather than a ribbon: the x axis is a set of levels, and there is nothing between them
   to interpolate.

   :param display: ``"grouped"`` splits the anatomical levels into a grid of panels (see
                   :mod:`nvitk.stats.region_groups`). The split follows whichever column holds them — *hue* when
                   there is one, otherwise *x*, in which case each panel's axis carries only its own levels.
                   The means themselves are unchanged: they were estimated over the whole model either way.
   :type display: {"overview", "grouped"}


.. py:function:: validate_mmrm_data(data: pandas.DataFrame, *, visit: str, subject: str, structure: str = 'us') -> list[str]

   Problems that would make an ``mmrm`` fit fail or mislead, as human-readable messages.

   ``mmrm`` requires at most one observation per ``(subject, visit)`` cell — the covariance matrix
   is indexed by visit, so a duplicate has no place to go and R raises a message that does not
   point at the data. Checking here means the error names the offending subjects.

.. py:function:: fit_lme4(*, data: pandas.DataFrame, formula: str, family: str = 'gaussian', reml: bool = True, control: str = '', dropna_columns: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> tuple[Any, pandas.DataFrame, dict[str, Any]]

   Fit ``lme4::lmer`` / ``glmer`` through ``pymer4``.

   :param formula: An lme4 formula, random terms included:
                   ``pi ~ age_c + (1 + age_c | territory) + (1 | subject_uid)``.
   :type formula: str
   :param family: ``gaussian`` uses ``lmer``; anything else (``binomial``, ``poisson``, ``gamma``,
                  ``inverse_gaussian``) uses ``glmer``.
   :type family: str
   :param reml: Restricted maximum likelihood. Leave it on for variance estimates; turn it off to compare
                models that differ in their *fixed* effects by likelihood, where REML fits are not
                comparable.
   :type reml: bool
   :param control: Raw ``lme4::lmerControl(...)`` string, for convergence trouble.
   :type control: str

   :returns: *model* is the ``pymer4`` ``Lmer``; *metadata* matches the other engines so the GUI's
             row-count reporting is identical.
   :rtype: (model, model_df, metadata)

   :raises RuntimeError: If the R backend is not available; the message names what is missing.


.. py:function:: lme4_coef_frame(model: Any) -> pandas.DataFrame

   ``pymer4``'s fixed-effects table normalized to this package's column names.

   0.9 puts it in ``.result_fit`` as a polars frame from easystats ``model_parameters()``, with the
   term names in a ``Parameter`` *column*; 0.8 put it in ``.coefs`` as a pandas frame with the terms
   in the index. Both are accepted.


.. py:function:: lme4_emmeans(model: Any, specs: str, *, at_name: str = '', at_values: Sequence[float] | None = None, ci_level: float = 0.95) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Estimated marginal means and their confidence intervals, from ``emmeans`` in R.

   ``lme4`` gives predictions but no standard errors, so this is what makes a confidence band on an
   lme4 plot possible at all.

   :param specs: An emmeans specification formula: ``"~ territory"``, or ``"~ age_c | territory"`` to get one
                 curve per level.
   :type specs: str
   :param at_name: Evaluate a *continuous* predictor over a grid — ``at_name="age_c"`` with the x values the
                   line is drawn at. Leave unset for a purely categorical specification.
   :param at_values: Evaluate a *continuous* predictor over a grid — ``at_name="age_c"`` with the x values the
                     line is drawn at. Leave unset for a purely categorical specification.
   :param ci_level: Confidence level for the returned interval.
   :type ci_level: float

   :returns: The grid columns plus ``emmean``, ``SE``, ``df``, ``lower.CL``, ``upper.CL``.
   :rtype: pandas.DataFrame


.. py:function:: lme4_fixed_formula(formula: str) -> str

   Strip the random terms from an ``lme4`` formula, leaving the fixed part.

   Needed to build a patsy design matrix for prediction grids: R holds the model, but the marginal
   means and their standard errors are computed on the Python side from the fixed-effects design.

   >>> lme4_fixed_formula("pi ~ age_c + (1 + age_c | territory) + (1 | subject_uid)")
   'pi ~ age_c'


.. py:function:: lme4_grouping_factors(formula: str) -> list[str]

   Grouping columns named on the right of each ``|`` in an ``lme4`` formula.


.. py:function:: lme4_info_dict(model: Any, *, outcome_name: str = 'Outcome', meta: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

   Report structure matching :func:`~nvitk.stats.mixedlm.mixedlm_info_dict`, from an ``Lmer``.


.. py:function:: lme4_predict(model: Any, grid: pandas.DataFrame, *, use_random_effects: bool = False) -> numpy.ndarray

   Predict on *grid* through ``pymer4``.

   ``use_random_effects`` selects between the population-level prediction and one that includes the
   fitted group deviations. 0.9 passes straight through to R's ``predict`` (where the switch is
   ``re.form=NA`` for population level); 0.8 spelled it ``use_rfx``. Each is tried in turn, so the
   call works on either.


.. py:function:: lme4_group_coefficients(model: Any) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Per-group coefficients of an ``lme4`` fit — each level's own intercept and slopes.

   ``lme4`` already computes both: ``coef()`` gives the total per level (what pymer4 stores as
   ``.fixef``) and ``ranef()`` the deviation from the population average (``.ranef``). With several
   grouping factors each is a mapping keyed by factor, so the ``factor`` column keeps them apart —
   a model with ``(1 + age_c | territory) + (1 | subject_uid)`` lists both here.

   :returns: ``factor``, ``level``, then ``<term>`` (total) and ``<term>_dev`` (deviation) per term.
             Empty when the model exposes neither.
   :rtype: pandas.DataFrame


.. py:function:: lme4_random_effects_frame(model: Any) -> pandas.DataFrame

   ``pymer4``'s variance components normalized to component/kind/var/sd.

   0.9 fills ``.ranef_var`` from ``broom.mixed::tidy(effects="ran_pars")``, which reports **standard
   deviations**, not variances — the terms are named ``sd__(Intercept)``, ``cor__…``,
   ``sd__Observation``. Squaring the SD to recover the variance (rather than reading ``estimate`` as
   one) is the difference between reporting 0.09 and 0.0084. Correlation rows are kept but marked,
   since squaring those would be meaningless.


.. py:function:: mixedlm_to_lme4_formula(formula: str, *, groups: str, re_formula: str = '1', vc_formula: Mapping[str, str] | None = None) -> str

   Translate a statsmodels MixedLM specification into one ``lme4`` formula.

   The three statsmodels arguments become bracketed random terms appended to the fixed part:

   * ``groups`` + ``re_formula`` → ``(<re_formula> | <groups>)``. ``re_formula="0"`` means no
     group-level random effect at all, so no term is emitted.
   * each ``vc_formula`` entry → ``(1 | <column>)``. A variance component written the statsmodels
     way, ``"0 + C(subject_uid)"``, is exactly lme4's ``(1 | subject_uid)``: one independent
     intercept per level.

   .. rubric:: Examples

   >>> mixedlm_to_lme4_formula(
   ...     "pi ~ age_c", groups="territory", re_formula="1 + age_c",
   ...     vc_formula={"subject": "0 + C(subject_uid)"})
   'pi ~ age_c + (1 + age_c | territory) + (1 | subject_uid)'


.. py:function:: plot_lme4_params(*, model: Any, df_fit: pandas.DataFrame, x: str, y: str, group: str = '', mode: str = 'auto', group_order: Sequence[str] | None = None, restrict_to_orders: bool = False, include_points: bool = True, errorbar: bool = False, ci_level: float = 0.95, fixed_formula: str = '', palette: str = 'tab10', display: str = 'overview', title: str = 'lme4', x_label: str | None = None, y_label: str | None = None, predict_fn: Any = None, band_fn: Any = None, population_label: str = 'Population (fixed effects)', excluded_points: pandas.DataFrame | None = None) -> Any

   Population and per-group curves for an ``lme4`` fit, predicted through ``pymer4``.

   Mirrors :func:`~nvitk.stats.mixedlm.plot_mixedlm_params` visually — dashed black population
   curve, one coloured curve per group, observed data in a lighter tone — but gets its numbers from
   R rather than from a locally rebuilt design matrix.

   :param errorbar: Draw confidence intervals. ``lme4``'s ``predict`` returns no standard error, so these come
                    from :func:`lme4_emmeans` — marginal means computed by ``emmeans`` in R. A band appears per
                    group when the grouping factor is in the fixed part of the formula, and one population band
                    otherwise. When emmeans cannot supply them the curves are still drawn and the figure carries
                    ``ci_error``.
   :type errorbar: bool
   :param fixed_formula: The formula's fixed part, used to decide whether the grouping factor has marginal means to
                         report level by level.
   :type fixed_formula: str
   :param display: ``"overview"`` puts every level on one pair of axes; ``"grouped"`` splits them into a grid of
                   anatomical panels (see :mod:`nvitk.stats.region_groups`), each autoscaled to its own range.
                   Both draw the same fit — the population curve and the emmeans intervals are computed once and
                   repeat across panels.
   :type display: {"overview", "grouped"}
   :param excluded_points: Observations a filter removed, drawn in grey beneath the kept ones. They are not in
                           *df_fit* — the fit ran on the filtered frame — so they have to be supplied separately.
   :type excluded_points: pandas.DataFrame, optional
   :param predict_fn: Engine hooks. They default to ``lme4``'s, and exist so another R engine whose parameters are
                      named by R rather than by patsy — :func:`~nvitk.stats.r_robust.plot_lmrob_params` — reuses
                      this drawing code instead of copying it. Not needed for ordinary ``lme4`` use.
   :param band_fn: Engine hooks. They default to ``lme4``'s, and exist so another R engine whose parameters are
                   named by R rather than by patsy — :func:`~nvitk.stats.r_robust.plot_lmrob_params` — reuses
                   this drawing code instead of copying it. Not needed for ordinary ``lme4`` use.
   :param population_label: Engine hooks. They default to ``lme4``'s, and exist so another R engine whose parameters are
                            named by R rather than by patsy — :func:`~nvitk.stats.r_robust.plot_lmrob_params` — reuses
                            this drawing code instead of copying it. Not needed for ordinary ``lme4`` use.


.. py:function:: r_backend_status(*, check_r_packages: bool = True) -> RBackendStatus

   Probe the whole Python → rpy2 → R → lme4 chain.

   Never raises and never imports R as a side effect of importing this module: the GUI calls it to
   decide whether to offer the engine at all, and a broken R installation must not take the window
   down with it.

   :param check_r_packages: Shell out to ``Rscript`` to check the R package versions. Skip it (a second or two) when you
                            only need to know whether the Python side is importable.
   :type check_r_packages: bool

.. py:function:: fit_glm(*, data: pandas.DataFrame, formula: str, family: str = 'gaussian', link: str | None = None, required_columns: Sequence[str] | None = None, dropna_columns: Sequence[str] | None = None, fit_kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> tuple[Any, pandas.DataFrame, dict[str, Any]]

   Fit a generalized linear model.

   The link is where the non-linearity lives: predictors combine linearly on the link scale, and
   the fitted values are mapped back through its inverse. Coefficients are therefore effects *on
   the link scale* — log-odds for a logit link, log-ratios for a log link.


.. py:function:: fit_nonlinear(*, data: pandas.DataFrame, x: str, y: str, model: str = 'exp_decay', p0: Sequence[float] | None = None, maxfev: int = 20000) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], pandas.DataFrame, dict[str, Any]]

   Fit an explicit parametric curve of *y* against *x* by non-linear least squares.

   Unlike the formula-driven engines this fits one predictor against one response, with no
   covariate adjustment and no grouping — the parameters are the model.

   :returns: *result* is a dict with ``params`` (a coefficient frame), ``predict`` (a callable),
             ``cov``, ``r_squared``, ``rmse``, ``n_obs`` and the model spec — not a statsmodels object,
             so it is handled separately by the reporting and plotting helpers.
   :rtype: (result, model_df, metadata)


.. py:function:: fit_ols(*, data: pandas.DataFrame, formula: str, required_columns: Sequence[str] | None = None, dropna_columns: Sequence[str] | None = None, robust: str | None = None, fit_kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> tuple[Any, pandas.DataFrame, dict[str, Any]]

   Fit an ordinary least squares model.

   :param robust: Heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance type (``"HC0"`` … ``"HC3"``). Worth setting when
                  the residual spread grows with the fitted value; it changes the standard errors, not the
                  coefficients.
   :type robust: str, optional

   :returns: Shaped like :func:`~nvitk.stats.mixedlm.fit_or_load_mixedlm` so callers are interchangeable.
   :rtype: (result, model_df, metadata)


.. py:function:: model_info_dict(result: Any, *, outcome_name: str = 'Outcome', group_name: str = 'Group', meta: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

   Structured report for **any** engine — MixedLM, OLS, GLM or non-linear.

   Dispatches on the result type so the GUI report panel and
   :func:`~nvitk.stats.mixedlm.render_mixedlm_info` need to know nothing about which model was run.


.. py:function:: nonlinear_confidence_band(result: Mapping[str, Any], grid: numpy.ndarray, *, ci_level: float = 0.95) -> tuple[numpy.ndarray, numpy.ndarray, numpy.ndarray]

   Fitted curve and its confidence band over *grid*, by the delta method.

   The gradient of the curve with respect to each parameter is taken numerically, then
   ``se(x) = √(gᵀ Σ g)`` propagates the parameter covariance to the prediction.

   :rtype: (fitted, lower, upper)


.. py:function:: plot_nonlinear_fit(result: Mapping[str, Any], data: pandas.DataFrame, *, errorbar: bool = False, ci_level: float = 0.95, include_points: bool = True, group: str | None = None, group_order: Sequence[str] | None = None, palette: str = 'tab10', display: str = 'overview', title: str | None = None, x_label: str | None = None, y_label: str | None = None) -> Any

   Scatter of the observations with the fitted curve, optionally with a confidence band.

   The curve is a single fit over all rows: *group* only colours the scatter, it does not fit one
   curve per group. Fitting per group would mean one non-linear fit per level, which the parameter
   table has no room to report honestly.

   :param display: ``"grouped"`` splits *group*'s levels into a grid of anatomical panels (see
                   :mod:`nvitk.stats.region_groups`), each autoscaled to its own range. The fitted curve is the
                   same single fit in every panel — which is exactly what makes the panels comparable: each one
                   shows how its own regions sit against the common curve.
   :type display: {"overview", "grouped"}


.. py:function:: prepare_model_frame(data: pandas.DataFrame, formula: str, *, required_columns: Sequence[str] | None = None, dropna_columns: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> tuple[pandas.DataFrame, dict[str, Any]]

   Sanitize column names, coerce object-numerics and drop incomplete rows.

   The same preparation :func:`~nvitk.stats.mixedlm.fit_or_load_mixedlm` performs, factored out so
   every engine reports row counts the same way and the GUI's "dropped N incomplete rows" note
   means the same thing whichever model was fitted.


.. py:function:: spline_term(kind: str, column: str, *, df: int = 4) -> str

   Render a :data:`SPLINE_TERMS` template, e.g. ``("bs", "age_c", df=4) -> "bs(age_c, df=4)"``.

.. py:function:: fit_lmrob(*, data: pandas.DataFrame, formula: str, method: str = 'MM', psi: str = 'bisquare', setting: str = '', max_iterations: int = 500, seed: int | None = 42) -> tuple[Any, pandas.DataFrame, dict[str, Any]]

   Fit a robust linear model by MM-estimation.

   :param formula: An R formula, e.g. ``"pi ~ age_c + sex + territory"``. There is no random part: ``lmrob``
                   fits a single population regression. For clustered data — repeated territories within a
                   subject — the coefficients stay valid but the standard errors ignore the clustering; use
                   ``lme4`` or MMRM when the correlation is the point.
   :type formula: str
   :param method: Estimation chain, see :data:`LMROB_ESTIMATORS`.
   :type method: str
   :param psi: Loss function, see :data:`LMROB_PSI`. Ignored when *setting* is given.
   :type psi: str
   :param setting: A published control preset. When set it overrides *method* and *psi*.
   :type setting: {"", "KS2011", "KS2014"}
   :param seed: The initial S-estimate resamples at random, so an unpinned seed makes the fit irreproducible
                at the last decimal. ``None`` leaves R's generator alone.
   :type seed: int or None

   :returns: *fit* is the R ``lmrob`` object. *model_df* is the frame actually fitted, in the same row
             order as the robustness weights. *metadata* matches the other engines.
   :rtype: (fit, model_df, metadata)


.. py:function:: lmrob_coef_frame(fit: Any, *, ci_level: float = 0.95) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Coefficient table in the shared shape: ``parameter coef std_err z p_value ci_low ci_high sig``.

   The standard errors are the robust ones ``summary.lmrob`` reports — computed from the estimator's
   own sandwich-type covariance, not from an OLS residual variance.


.. py:function:: lmrob_emmeans(fit: Any, specs: str, *, at_name: str = '', at_values: Sequence[float] | None = None, ci_level: float = 0.95) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Estimated marginal means and their confidence intervals, from ``emmeans`` in R.

   Same signature and return shape as :func:`~nvitk.stats.r_mixedlm.lme4_emmeans`, so the shared
   plotting code can call either. It reuses that module's R helper, which takes any model
   ``emmeans`` supports — and ``emmeans`` supports ``lmrob`` directly. The one difference is that
   an ``lmrob`` fit *is* the R object, where a pymer4 model wraps one.

   :param specs: An emmeans specification formula: ``"~ territory"``, or ``"~ age_c | territory"``.
   :type specs: str
   :param at_name: Evaluate a continuous predictor over a grid, for a confidence band along a line.
   :param at_values: Evaluate a continuous predictor over a grid, for a confidence band along a line.


.. py:function:: lmrob_info_dict(fit: Any, *, outcome_name: str = 'Outcome', group_name: str = 'Group', meta: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

   Structured report in the same shape the other engines return, for the GUI report panel.


.. py:function:: lmrob_weights_frame(fit: Any, model_df: pandas.DataFrame | None = None, *, key_columns: Sequence[str] = ()) -> pandas.DataFrame

   Per-observation robustness weights — the diagnostic that makes a robust fit worth running.

   A weight of 1 means the observation was treated as ordinary; 0 means the estimator rejected it
   outright. Joining the low-weight rows back to *model_df* names the subject and territory behind
   each one, which is normally a shortlist of scans to re-inspect rather than a statistical finding.

   :param model_df: The frame returned by :func:`fit_lmrob`, in its original row order. Its *key_columns* are
                    attached to the weights so each row is identifiable.
   :type model_df: pandas.DataFrame, optional
   :param key_columns: Which columns to carry over — typically ``("subject_uid", "territory")``. Defaults to those
                       two when they are present.
   :type key_columns: sequence of str

   :returns: ``weight``, ``residual``, ``fitted``, ``rejected``, plus the key columns, sorted by weight so
             the most heavily discounted observations come first.
   :rtype: pandas.DataFrame


.. py:function:: plot_lmrob_params(*, fit: Any, df_fit: pandas.DataFrame, x: str, y: str, group: str = '', mode: str = 'auto', group_order: Sequence[str] | None = None, restrict_to_orders: bool = False, include_points: bool = True, errorbar: bool = False, ci_level: float = 0.95, fixed_formula: str = '', palette: str = 'tab10', display: str = 'overview', title: str = 'Robust linear model', x_label: str | None = None, y_label: str | None = None) -> Any

   Population and per-level curves for a robust fit, predicted through R.

   Visually identical to the other engines' plots — dashed black population curve, one coloured
   curve per level, observed data in a lighter tone — and it supports the same
   ``display="grouped"`` anatomical panelling. The per-level curves only separate when the grouping
   factor is in the formula: ``lmrob`` has no random effects to place them apart otherwise.


.. py:function:: plot_lmrob_weights(weights: pandas.DataFrame, *, label_column: str = '', threshold: float = 0.5, max_labels: int = 25, title: str = 'Robustness weights') -> Any

   Weight against fitted value, with the discounted observations labelled.

   Reading it: a cloud at weight 1 with a short tail is a well-behaved fit; a long tail, or a
   cluster of low weights sharing one territory, says the model and that territory disagree — which
   is either a real subgroup or a segmentation problem, and worth knowing which.


.. py:function:: robust_backend_status(*, check_r_packages: bool = True) -> RobustBackendStatus

   Probe rpy2 → R → ``robustbase``. Never raises, and never imports R as an import side effect.

   Independent of the lme4 and MMRM probes: ``robustbase`` has no shared dependency with either, so
   it can be available when they are not.

.. py:function:: summarize_by_group(frame: pandas.DataFrame, column: str, *, by: str | Sequence[str] = '', ci: float = 0.95, include_overall: bool = True, sort_by: str = 'group') -> pandas.DataFrame

   Descriptive statistics of *column*, one row per group of *by*.

   :param by: Grouping column(s). Several are combined into one label (``Left_ICA | male``) rather than a
              MultiIndex, so the sheet stays flat and readable. Empty summarises the column as a whole.
   :type by: str or sequence of str
   :param include_overall: Append an :data:`OVERALL_LABEL` row over every group. Worth having in the same table — a
                           per-territory mean is usually read against the whole-cohort one.
   :type include_overall: bool
   :param sort_by: Row order. ``"group"`` sorts naturally, so ``g2`` precedes ``g10``.
   :type sort_by: {"group", "mean", "median", "n"}

   :returns: Columns as in :data:`SUMMARY_COLUMNS`. ``frame.attrs`` carries ``column``, ``by`` and
             ``ci`` so an exporter can label the sheet without being told again.
   :rtype: pandas.DataFrame

   :raises ValueError: When *column* or a grouping column is absent, or *column* holds nothing numeric.

   many rows it came from is unreconstructable a month later — including by its author.

.. py:function:: available_presets(columns: Sequence[str], *, column: str = '') -> list[tuple[QcFilterPreset, str]]

   Every applicable preset, with whether the frame can satisfy it.

   The second element is ``"ready"`` when the metric column is in the frame and ``"unavailable"``
   otherwise. The metrics are **read from the dataset**, never derived here: scoring on the fly
   would give one session's filter a different answer from the published one, and from every other
   session — the QC has to mean the same thing everywhere it is read. Run the qvtpy stage 9 to
   publish them.

   Returned rather than filtered so the menu can grey an entry out with a reason; silently omitting
   it leaves the user wondering where the QC filters went.

   :param column: The column the menu was opened on. A preset tied to a specific measurement is only offered
                  there; the rest are offered anywhere, since they filter the frame rather than that column.
   :type column: str


.. py:function:: preset_rules(key: str, frame: pandas.DataFrame, *, threshold: float | None = None) -> list[nvitk.stats.frame_ops.FilterRule]

   Rules for one preset, validated against *frame*.

   :raises KeyError: Unknown preset.
   :raises ValueError: The frame lacks a column the preset needs — with the reason, since "run stage 9" is the
       actionable answer and an empty filter would silently do nothing.


.. py:data:: COMBINE_MODES

.. py:data:: COMBINE_OPS

.. py:class:: RegionCombination

   One quantity built by combining a measurement across regions.

   ``terms`` maps a region label to its coefficient, so ``{"Left_ICA": 1, "Right_ICA": 1,
   "Basilar": 1}`` with ``op="sum"`` is total cerebral blood flow, and ``{"Left_VA": 1,
   "Right_VA": 1, "Basilar": -1}`` is the vertebrobasilar mass-balance residual.


   .. py:attribute:: name
      :type:  str


   .. py:attribute:: value_column
      :type:  str


   .. py:attribute:: terms
      :type:  Mapping[str, float]


   .. py:attribute:: op
      :type:  str
      :value: 'sum'



   .. py:attribute:: mode
      :type:  str
      :value: 'column'



   .. py:attribute:: region_column
      :type:  str
      :value: 'territory'



   .. py:attribute:: subject_column
      :type:  str
      :value: 'subject_uid'



   .. py:attribute:: require_all
      :type:  bool
      :value: True



   .. py:attribute:: unit
      :type:  str
      :value: ''



   .. py:attribute:: description
      :type:  str
      :value: ''



   .. py:method:: validate() -> str

      Empty when the combination is well-formed, otherwise the reason it is not.



   .. py:method:: expression() -> str

      The combination as readable text, for a label or a tooltip.



   .. py:method:: to_dict() -> dict[str, Any]

      Config-serializable form.



   .. py:method:: from_dict(data: Mapping[str, Any]) -> RegionCombination
      :classmethod:


      Rebuild from :meth:`to_dict`, tolerating keys an older config did not have.



.. py:function:: apply_region_combinations(df: pandas.DataFrame, combinations: Sequence[RegionCombination]) -> tuple[pandas.DataFrame, list[str], list[dict[str, Any]]]

   Apply each combination to a copy of *df*, in order.

   ``mode="column"`` merges the per-subject value back onto every row of that subject, so it can be
   used as a covariate beside the per-territory outcome. ``mode="row"`` appends synthetic rows
   carrying the combination's name as their region, so it can be modelled as another territory —
   note those rows are **not independent** of the ones they were built from, which matters if the
   model treats territories as replicates.

   A combination that fails is skipped with its error collected, so one bad definition does not
   cost the rest.

   :rtype: (frame, errors, reports)


.. py:function:: composite_combinations(value_column: str = 'flow_mean', *, region_column: str = 'territory', subject_column: str = 'subject_uid') -> list[RegionCombination]

   The standard whole-brain composites: total inflow, and the anterior/posterior split.

   ``TCBF`` is the one asked for most often — total cerebral blood flow as the sum of both internal
   carotids and the basilar. It is a *column*, not a territory: it is the subject's total, so it
   belongs beside the per-territory rows rather than among them.


.. py:function:: conservation_combinations(value_column: str = 'flow_mean', *, region_column: str = 'territory', subject_column: str = 'subject_uid', rules: Sequence[str] | None = None, relative: bool = False) -> list[RegionCombination]

   The mass-balance rules as ready-to-apply combinations.

   This is the answer to "how do I get conservation residuals as derived columns": each rule in
   :data:`~nvitk.stats.vessel_network.CONSERVATION_RULES` is already a weighted sum over regions,
   so it maps directly onto a :class:`RegionCombination` with ``op="sum"``. The result is one
   column per balance, on every row of the subject, ready to use as an outcome or a covariate.

   :param relative: Emit the balance as a *share* of the rule's inflow instead of an absolute residual.
                    Absolute residuals scale with cardiac output; relative ones are comparable between subjects.
   :type relative: bool


.. py:function:: evaluate_region_combination(df: pandas.DataFrame, combo: RegionCombination) -> tuple[pandas.Series, dict[str, Any]]

   Compute one combination, returning a per-subject series and a report of what it used.

   :returns: *values* is indexed by subject. *report* carries ``matched``, ``missing``,
             ``n_subjects``, ``n_incomplete`` and ``expression``.
   :rtype: (values, report)

   :raises ValueError: When the combination is malformed, its columns are absent, or no listed region is in the
       frame at all.


.. py:data:: COLLATERAL_SPECS

.. py:data:: CONSERVATION_RULES
